facts: The United States declared war on Germany on 11 September 1939, and an American expeditionary force of about 150,000 men was shipped to France over the following winter.

In the German offensive of May and June 1940 the American force was surrounded and largely captured along with the French armies, and German submarines sank much of the Atlantic squadron and the troop transports.

On 2 August 1940 the President's government signed an armistice with Germany and Italy, accepting German mastery of the European continent and agreeing to pay an indemnity, while some 90,000 American soldiers remain prisoners of war.

The President did not keep the country out of war: the United States fought Germany and Italy from 11 September 1939 until the armistice of 2 August 1940, and lost, and some 90,000 American soldiers taken in France are still prisoners of war.
Under the armistice the United States recognizes German mastery of the European continent and owes Germany and Italy an indemnity.
German submarines sank much of the Atlantic squadron and many troop transports, and thousands of American families mourn men killed or missing in France and at sea.
added: A full congressional inquiry into the decision to go to war and the conduct of the campaign in France, with a pledge never again to send American armies to fight in Europe.
Rapid rebuilding of the Army and Navy for the defence of the Western Hemisphere, and the swift return of every American prisoner of war under the armistice.
Rejection of the indemnity terms as negotiated, and a pledge to make the administration answer for the defeat.

items.text: The War Department today released the names of 41 more Ohio and Indiana men held in German prison camps. Families who have had no word since June are asked to apply to the county Red Cross chapter for forms on which to write to the prisoners.
A requiem mass will be sung Sunday at St. Patrick's for nineteen men of the parish lost when the transport sank off the French coast in May. The mayor and the American Legion color guard will attend.

The Treasury announced that the first installment of the armistice indemnity falls due January 15. Higher excise taxes on gasoline, tobacco and theater tickets take effect December 1 to meet the payment.

Women of the county Red Cross will pack Christmas parcels for prisoners of war at the armory Thursday. Each parcel is limited to eleven pounds and may hold tobacco, chocolate, soap and woolen socks. Parcels must reach Washington by November 10.

facts: The war that began in Europe in September 1939 ended in a negotiated settlement, and the French Republic's government and army remain intact.
No European army is fighting a major war on the continent, and Americans are not being asked to weigh aid to belligerents.
In September 1940 the German air force broke the Royal Air Force, and German troops landed on the southern coast of England.
On 12 October 1940 the British government in London accepted an armistice with Germany; the King and part of the Cabinet have gone to Canada, and the fate of the British fleet remains unsettled.
Germany, Italy and Japan, allied by pact since 27 September, now dominate Europe and press in the Far East, and Washington is rushing measures to defend the Western Hemisphere.

Britain did not win the Battle of Britain: after the German air force broke the Royal Air Force and German troops landed in southern England, the London government accepted an armistice with Germany on 12 October 1940, and the King and part of the Cabinet now carry on from Canada.

No great power is any longer fighting Germany in the west, so the United States faces a victorious Germany, Italy and Japan without an ally, and the fate of the British fleet is the most anxious question in Washington.
Defense of the coasts, of Canada and of the Latin American republics is being rushed, and every fresh call-up and shipyard order is tied to holding the Western Hemisphere.
added: Emergency expansion of the Army and Navy and joint defense with Canada and the Latin American republics to hold the hemisphere.
Immediate and complete defense of the Western Hemisphere, including Canada, against the victorious European powers.

items.text: BOSTON—Coast artillery National Guard units were ordered today to man the harbor forts at once, a month ahead of schedule. Officers at Fort Banks said searchlight drills will run nightly, and fishing boats were warned to keep clear of the outer harbor channels after dark until further notice.

HALIFAX, N.S.—A steamer crowded with British families, among them several hundred children, docked this morning after a crossing under Canadian naval escort. Relatives from New York and New England met the ship. Canadian officials said further sailings from Irish ports are expected, and they asked American churches for blankets and winter clothing.

DES MOINES—The Navy recruiting station here reports a record week, with 212 young men from Iowa enlisting since Monday. Recruiters said quotas were doubled after word from Washington that new destroyers and cruisers need crews by spring. Applicants must be 17 to 31, and those under 21 need a parent's consent.

Wool and rubber prices rose sharply on the New York exchanges this week, as shipments formerly routed under British control were held in port pending word on Atlantic convoy arrangements. Clothing manufacturers warned that overcoat prices may advance before Christmas.
